What the new mining law actually does

The Ministry of Mines and Energy formally filed the “Ley Minera para la Transición Energética Justa, la Reindustrialización Nacional y la Minería para la Vida” in Congress on 1 October 2025. The bill, identified as Proyecto de Ley No.

282 de 2025 – Senado, arrived after more than a year of public consultation on earlier drafts.

Its stated purpose is to align mining with a just energy transition, national reindustrialisation, and what the government calls “mining for life.” The text puts mining at the service of human rights, food sovereignty, and nature protection, while reasserting state sovereignty over minerals.

In practice, the bill replaces the open concession logic of Ley 685 de 2001 with a planned model. It introduces Zones Apt for Mining (Zonas Aptas para la Minería, or ZAMs) defined through territorial and community participation, and it requires an integral environmental license starting from the exploration phase.

The state monopoly on strategic minerals

Article 27 of the new mining law is the provision drawing the sharpest reaction from industry. It states that only state-owned companies, mixed-economy enterprises, or “asociaciones público-populares” may explore and produce strategic minerals.

Private participation is permitted only if the State proves it lacks capacity, and even then under restrictive conditions. Juan Camilo Nariño, president of the Colombian Mining Association (ACM), calls this a de facto state monopoly that would severely limit private investment.

The government defends the approach as ensuring permanent state participation in strategic mineral projects. For investors holding existing titles, the shift raises immediate questions about asset security and the risk of what industry lawyers describe as indirect expropriation.

Environmental red lines and where mining is banned

The bill affirms the priority of water and environmental protection and expressly bans mining in páramos, national parks, Ramsar wetlands, mangroves, and other strategic ecosystems. It also introduces grounds to exclude areas for environmental, cultural, and social reasons.

The requirement for an environmental license from the exploration phase onward marks a significant departure from the previous staged approach. Industry groups argue the expanded exclusion zones and discretionary territorial decisions amount to an indiscriminate expansion of no-go areas.

For companies with existing concessions in areas that may be reclassified, the bill creates immediate uncertainty. The ACM warns that some existing titles could be effectively nullified through the new zoning process.

Royalties, fees, and the fiscal uncertainty

The new mining law adjusts the procedure for liquidating royalties and the surface fee (canon superficiario). It also introduces new obligations, including payment on stock-exchange gains related to mineral production.

A critical detail for investors is that 57 articles are left to be developed by subsequent regulation. Legal analysts warn this includes important aspects of the fiscal regime, creating a source of uncertainty about how royalties and related obligations will ultimately operate.

The bill also strengthens state powers to verify production volumes and enforce royalty payment. Combined with new causes for terminating titles and the abandonment of previous warning-before-sanction procedures, the enforcement regime becomes considerably tougher.

What the new mining law means for investors and expats

The ACM’s assessment is blunt: if the law passes as written, no company would want to invest or keep investing in Colombia. The combination of restricted private participation, expanded exclusion zones, and regulatory uncertainty is seen as a near-total deterrent to new projects.

For portfolio investors, the bill introduces risk across Colombian extractive equities and sovereign debt. The mining sector has been a reliable source of export revenues and fiscal income; a sharp contraction would have macroeconomic consequences.

Expats and professionals in the sector face a shifting landscape. The bill prioritises ethnic communities, traditional miners, and state-owned enterprises in mining zones, while private companies become exceptional participants.

Formalisation pathways for artisanal and small-scale miners are included, but transition timelines remain undefined.

The political path ahead

The bill now moves through Congress, where President Gustavo Petro‘s government will need to build coalitions to pass the 255-article text. The formal mining industry, led by the ACM, is mobilising against key provisions, particularly the strategic minerals monopoly.

Fenalcarbón, the national coal producers’ federation, has offered a more nuanced view, calling aspects of the environmental and territorial ordering “interesting and necessary.” But it warns that splitting resource administration across two laws confuses the reform’s essential aims.

The legislative debate will test whether the government can reconcile its vision of mining for life with the investment climate needed to fund it. For now, the market is watching and waiting.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Colombia’s new mining law?

It is a 255-article bill filed in Congress on 1 October 2025 by the Ministry of Mines and Energy. Officially titled “Ley Minera para la Transición Energética Justa, la Reindustrialización Nacional y la Minería para la Vida,” it replaces the concession model of Ley 685 de 2001 with a state-led, environmentally-planned mining framework.

How does the new mining law affect foreign investors?

The bill reserves strategic minerals for state-owned companies and limits private participation to cases where the State lacks capacity. Industry groups warn this creates a de facto state monopoly, deters new investment, and raises legal uncertainty.

Expanded environmental exclusion zones and 57 articles left to future regulation add further risk for existing and prospective investors.

Where does the new mining law ban mining?

The bill expressly bans mining in páramos, national parks, Ramsar wetlands, mangroves, and other strategic ecosystems. It also introduces grounds to exclude areas for environmental, cultural, and social reasons, and requires an environmental license from the exploration phase onward for all permitted projects.

World.title: Grupo Mexico Train Derailment Triggers Toxic Spill in Sonora
World.content:
Mining & Infrastructure

Key Facts —The Spill. A Ferromex train operated by Grupo Mexico derailed in Sonora, releasing roughly 59,000 litres of sodium hydrosulfide. —The Chemical. Sodium hydrosulfide is a toxic industrial compound that can release dangerous hydrogen sulfide gas upon contact with water or acids. —Immediate Response. Local authorities ordered evacuations and shelter-in-place protocols for nearby communities while hazmat teams deployed to the site. —Corporate Context. Grupo Mexico’s rail subsidiary Ferromex is the country’s largest freight operator, moving heavy minerals and chemicals across key industrial corridors. —Safety Record. The incident adds to a string of derailments and spills that have drawn scrutiny from regulators and communities along Mexico’s mining freight routes.

A Grupo Mexico train derailment in Sonora state has spilled an estimated 59,000 litres of sodium hydrosulfide, forcing evacuations and reigniting debate over the safety of the country’s mining supply chains.

What Happened in the Sonora Derailment

A Ferromex freight train operated by Grupo Mexico Transportes derailed along a key industrial route in Sonora. The accident ruptured tanker cars carrying sodium hydrosulfide, releasing approximately 59,000 litres of the hazardous chemical.

Sodium hydrosulfide is used extensively in mining and leather processing. It poses a serious inhalation risk because it can generate hydrogen sulfide gas, which is toxic even at low concentrations.

State civil protection authorities confirmed the spill and activated emergency protocols. No fatalities were immediately reported, but the full extent of environmental damage remains under assessment.

Evacuations and Emergency Response

Authorities ordered precautionary evacuations in a radius around the derailment site. Residents in several small communities were told to shelter in place and seal windows against potential gas exposure.

Specialised hazmat teams deployed to contain the spill and monitor air quality. Mexican army units with disaster-response training were also mobilised to support the operation.

The immediate challenge for responders was preventing the chemical from contacting water sources. Runoff into local waterways could magnify the environmental and public-health impact significantly.

The Mining division is involved in the operation of underground and open pit mines, smelters, refineries, and other plants. This division also provides copper, silver, molybdenum, zinc, sulfuric acid, gold, and selenium products. The Transportation division…

Grupo Mexico’s Dominance and Past Incidents

Grupo Mexico is one of the world’s largest copper producers and its transport arm, Ferromex, controls the country’s most extensive rail network. The company moves vast quantities of minerals, chemicals, and fuel daily.

This is not the first serious incident on its network. Previous derailments and chemical spills have drawn fines and criticism from Mexican environmental regulators and community groups.

The company has consistently stated it follows all safety protocols and cooperates fully with investigations. It has also invested in track upgrades, though critics argue the pace is too slow for the volume of hazardous freight.

The Chemical Risk: Sodium Hydrosulfide Explained

Sodium hydrosulfide (NaHS) is a corrosive, yellowish solid often transported in solution. It is a critical reagent in mining for separating copper and molybdenum ores.

The danger escalates when the chemical mixes with acidic water or moisture. This reaction releases hydrogen sulfide, a gas that smells of rotten eggs and can paralyse the respiratory system at high concentrations.

Long-term exposure at lower levels can cause chronic respiratory issues and eye damage. The Sonora spill’s proximity to populated areas makes the containment effort especially urgent.

Market and Supply-Chain Read-Through

Grupo Mexico’s shares on the Mexican stock exchange (BMV: GMEXICO B) are likely to face pressure as investors assess potential liabilities and operational disruptions. The company’s integrated mining-to-rail model means any transport interruption can ripple back to mine output.

For global copper markets, a prolonged disruption on this freight corridor would tighten supply chains already strained by growing demand for electrification. Sonora is a vital artery for moving Mexican copper to Pacific ports for export to Asia.

Insurers and reinsurers covering hazardous-freight rail in Latin America will also be watching closely. A major claim could harden premiums across the sector, raising logistics costs for all mining operators in the region.

Regulatory and Political Fallout

Mexico’s environmental protection agency (PROFEPA) and the communications and transport ministry (SICT) have opened a joint investigation. Early findings will focus on track integrity, train speed, and maintenance records.

The incident is likely to intensify calls in Congress for stricter oversight of hazardous-material rail shipments. Community groups in Sonora have long demanded real-time monitoring and tougher emergency-response requirements.

For expats and foreign investors with assets in northern Mexico, the spill is a reminder of the physical risks embedded in the country’s industrial infrastructure. Environmental liability is an increasingly material factor in Mexican due diligence.

What to Watch Next

The immediate priority is the completion of the containment and air-quality assessments. Authorities will decide when evacuated residents can safely return, a process that could take days.

Grupo Mexico will need to issue a detailed statement on the cause and its remediation plan. The company’s transparency in the coming days will heavily influence market reaction and regulatory tone.

Longer term, watch for any new legislation on hazardous-freight routing or mandatory investment in track safety technology. This derailment could become the catalyst for a regulatory shift that reshapes logistics costs across Mexico’s mining sector.

Frequently Asked Questions

What chemical was spilled in the Grupo Mexico train derailment in Sonora?

The derailed Ferromex train spilled approximately 59,000 litres of sodium hydrosulfide, a toxic industrial chemical used mainly in mining operations. It can release dangerous hydrogen sulfide gas when it contacts water or acids.

Were there evacuations after the Sonora chemical spill?

Yes, local civil protection authorities ordered evacuations and shelter-in-place orders for communities near the derailment site. Hazmat teams and military units were deployed to contain the spill and monitor air quality.

How might this derailment affect Grupo Mexico’s business?

The spill could pressure Grupo Mexico’s share price and trigger regulatory fines. A prolonged disruption on this key freight corridor may also impact copper supply chains and raise insurance costs for hazardous-material rail transport across Latin America.

World.title: Argentina’s Central Bank Pauses Dollar-Buying Streak After IMF Praise
World.content:
Argentina · Monetary Policy

Key Facts —The pause. The BCRA did not buy dollars on 28 July 2026, ending a 135-session streak that began on 2 January 2026. —Reserve build-up. The central bank accumulated roughly US$13 billion in gross reserves during the nearly seven-month buying streak. —Gross reserves level. Gross foreign reserves stood at US$48.391 billion at the close of trading on the pause day. —IMF encouragement. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva visited Buenos Aires days before and explicitly told authorities to “keep buying” dollars. —Peso management. The pause was partly tactical, aimed at keeping the wholesale dollar from breaching the ARS 1,500 per US$ threshold.

Argentina’s central bank ended its historic dollar-buying streak on Tuesday, pausing after 135 consecutive sessions of purchases that added US$13 billion to reserves, just days after the IMF chief visited Buenos Aires and praised the accumulation programme.

A 135-session dollar-buying streak comes to a tactical halt

The Banco Central de la República Argentina (BCRA) stepped back from the foreign-exchange market on 28 July 2026, breaking a run of daily dollar purchases that had stretched unbroken since 2 January. The central bank confirmed it made no intervention, citing heavy buying by energy-sector firms that supplied enough dollars to the market without official participation.

The pause was not a policy reversal but a calculated move to prevent the wholesale peso from weakening past the closely watched ARS 1,500 per US$ line. The wholesale exchange rate closed the session at ARS 1,499.84, barely inside the threshold that authorities have defended under the crawling-peg regime.

By halting purchases, the BCRA also slowed the injection of pesos into the economy, a side effect of its reserve-building that requires the Treasury to absorb excess liquidity through regular debt auctions. The decision highlighted the balancing act between shoring up reserves and maintaining exchange-rate stability.

Reserves surge to near US$49 billion on the back of aggressive buying

The BCRA’s sustained intervention transformed the country’s reserve position over the first seven months of 2026. Gross foreign reserves reached US$48.391 billion on the day of the pause, a level not seen since 2019, after starting the year significantly lower.

The accumulation averaged roughly US$98 million per day, with several outsized sessions punctuating the trend. A single-day jump of over US$1.2 billion on 7 July pushed gross reserves to US$49.536 billion, while a US$532 million purchase on 14 July marked the largest daily acquisition since late 2022.

By late July, year-to-date net purchases had surpassed US$13.1 billion, comfortably exceeding the BCRA’s annual goal of US$10 billion. The reserve build-up has been a cornerstone of President Javier Milei’s economic programme, aimed at rebuilding credibility with international creditors and eventually dismantling capital controls.

IMF chief visits Buenos Aires and says “keep buying”

The pause came just days after IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva visited Buenos Aires and delivered a clear message on the reserve programme. Speaking during her late-July trip, Georgieva praised Argentina’s shift from fiscal deficit to primary surplus and the decline in annual inflation from over 200 percent in late 2023 to around 32.5 percent by early 2026.

She pointed specifically to the US$13 billion in reserve accumulation since January and told authorities to “keep buying.” The Fund had already modified Argentina’s net-international-reserves target earlier in 2026, effectively instructing the Milei government to continue the dollar-purchase programme while maintaining some exchange-rate flexibility.

Net reserves rose by about US$7 billion under the programme, putting Argentina very close to its US$8 billion end-2026 target under the IMF agreement. The Fund’s public endorsement signalled confidence that the buying streak, even with its tactical pauses, remains aligned with programme objectives.

The peso tightrope: crawling-peg discipline meets market pressure

The official peso has been managed through small daily depreciations under a crawling-peg policy, keeping it at the very top of its 52-week range. On the day of the pause, the official rate stood at ARS 1,497 per US$, virtually unchanged, before weakening 0.18 percent to ARS 1,500 the following session.

The tight management of the official rate contrasts with persistent premia in parallel markets. By mid-July, the blue dollar traded between ARS 1,510 and ARS 1,530, while the MEP dollar sat at about ARS 1,514 and the CCL dollar reached roughly ARS 1,560, reflecting continued demand for financial-dollar hedges.

The Merval stock index rose 0.65 percent to 3,305,316 points on the pause day, as markets digested the tactical shift without alarm. Investors appeared to treat the halt as a routine operational adjustment rather than a signal of stress in the FX programme.

What the dollar-buying streak pause means for investors and expats

For international investors, the pause reinforces that Argentina’s reserve-building strategy is pragmatic rather than dogmatic. The BCRA has shown it will step aside when private-sector flows are sufficient, prioritising exchange-rate stability over mechanical accumulation.

The broader trajectory remains one of reserve strengthening, which improves Argentina’s capacity to meet external obligations and edges the country closer to lifting capital controls. Expats and businesses operating in Argentina should expect the crawling-peg to persist, with the official peso continuing its gradual, controlled depreciation.

The key risk to watch is whether the BCRA can resume purchases without pushing the wholesale rate decisively above ARS 1,500. A sustained breach would test the central bank’s commitment to the crawling-peg framework and could trigger a faster pace of depreciation, with knock-on effects for inflation and parallel exchange rates.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Argentina’s central bank pause its dollar-buying streak?

The BCRA paused purchases on 28 July 2026 for two stated reasons. Strong dollar buying by energy companies provided sufficient FX supply that day, and the central bank wanted to prevent the wholesale peso from weakening past the ARS 1,500 per US$ threshold.

The pause also slowed the injection of pesos into the economy, reducing the need for the Treasury to absorb liquidity through debt auctions.

How much did Argentina’s reserves grow during the dollar-buying streak?

The BCRA accumulated roughly US$13.128 billion in gross reserves between 2 January and 28 July 2026, averaging about US$98 million per day across 135 consecutive sessions. Gross foreign reserves reached US$48.391 billion on the pause day, the highest level since 2019, comfortably exceeding the central bank’s US$10 billion annual accumulation goal.

What did the IMF say about Argentina’s reserve-buying programme?

IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva visited Buenos Aires in late July 2026 and explicitly encouraged authorities to “keep buying” dollars. She highlighted the US$13 billion reserve accumulation, the shift to a primary fiscal surplus, and the drop in annual inflation from about 210 percent to around 30 percent.

The Fund noted Argentina was very close to its US$8 billion net-international-reserves target for end-2026.

World.title: Milei’s Central-Bank Reform Would Ban Argentina’s Money-Printing
World.content:
Argentina Policy

Key Facts —Announcement. President Milei will detail the BCRA charter reform in a national broadcast on 30 July 2026. —Single Mandate. The bill proposes restoring the Central Bank’s sole mission to preserving the currency’s value. —Financing Ban. It explicitly prohibits BCRA financing of the national government, provinces, and municipalities. —Privatisation Path. The separate Ley de Bases framework already authorises the sale of eight state-owned companies. —IMF Alignment. The Fund has explicitly requested the charter reform to strengthen institutional independence.

Argentina central bank reform will enter Congress in early August 2026, as President Javier Milei seeks to constitutionally ban monetary financing of the state and enshrine a single mandate for the peso, while a parallel privatisation drive advances under existing law.

The Core of the Argentina Central Bank Reform

President Milei will outline the project in a pre-recorded national address on 30 July 2026 at 20:00 local time. The government then plans to send the legislation to Congress in the first days of August, though it has not yet decided whether the Senate or the Chamber of Deputies will debate it first.

The central pillar is a return to a single legal mandate for the BCRA: preserving the value of the currency. This would undo the 2012 reform that gave the bank multiple objectives, including employment and financial stability, which Milei calls a “declaration of ignorance.”

The bill explicitly prohibits the Central Bank from financing the State at any level. This covers the National Treasury, provincial governments, municipalities, and any primary-market purchase of public debt, effectively ending the practice of “adelantos transitorios” that historically funded deficits.

Governance, Independence, and the End of Letras Intransferibles

The reform strengthens institutional firewalls around the BCRA’s leadership. Removing the governor or board directors would require a two-thirds majority in both houses of Congress, a high bar designed to insulate monetary policy from political cycles.

A version under study also mandates Senate consent for appointments and removals of directors. The project further eliminates the 2012 charter changes and abolishes non-transferable Treasury letters, the instruments that swapped BCRA reserves for illiquid government paper for years.

On profits, valuation gains from price changes would be locked in a non-distributable technical reserve. Only results from active portfolio management could flow to the Treasury, and solely to cancel existing debt, closing a long-standing loophole.

A Second Phase: Criminal Penalties and Shutdown Mechanisms

The government is considering splitting the package to improve its legislative chances. A second tranche of bills would address the criminalisation of monetary issuance to fund the deficit, treating it as counterfeiting under the Penal Code.

This follow-up package would also introduce a “shutdown” mechanism. It would restrict or halt State operations when budget appropriations are exhausted, reinforcing the administration’s commitment to a zero-deficit rule.

As of late July 2026, this second legislative tranche has no fixed submission date. Officials indicate it may arrive within the second half of the year, giving the government time to build a coalition for the more contentious provisions.

The Privatisation Track: Ley de Bases in Action

While the BCRA reform grabs headlines, the privatisation of state-owned enterprises runs on a separate, already-operational track. The Ley de Bases, Law 27,742 of 2024, provides the legal framework for total or partial sale of eight public companies.

The U.S. State Department’s 2025 Investment Climate Statement confirms the law aims to optimise resource allocation and reduce the fiscal burden of SOEs. An IMF staff report names Aerolíneas Argentinas, Energía Argentina, Radio y Televisión Argentina, Intercargo, and water utility AySA among the entities up for privatisation.

Four companies are already in the active privatisation pipeline, with five more under consideration. This process is not tied directly to the BCRA charter bill but forms part of the broader stabilisation programme that Milei is pursuing with IMF backing.

Political Reactions and the IMF Factor

A group of former BCRA presidents criticised the reform, arguing a single mandate is too narrow and rigid. Milei responded on 2 July by calling them “economic illiterates” and insisting the multi-objective framework allowed emission “for anything.”

The IMF has explicitly requested reform of the BCRA charter as part of its conditionality framework. Milei presents the project as fully aligned with the Fund’s requirements, which strengthens its credibility with international investors watching Argentina’s stabilisation effort.

The government remains uncertain of legislative support and is holding intensive briefing sessions with La Libertad Avanza legislators. Splitting the package into more digestible parts is the clearest signal yet that the administration is prepared to negotiate rather than gamble on a single high-stakes vote.

What the Argentina Central Bank Reform Means for Investors and Expats

For foreign investors, the reform is a structural signal. A legally independent Central Bank with a single mandate and no obligation to fund the Treasury removes a primary driver of Argentina’s chronic inflation, which averaged over 100% annually in recent years.

The parallel privatisation pipeline offers concrete opportunities in transport, energy, media, and utilities. The Ley de Bases framework provides a legal entry point for private capital, and the IMF’s involvement adds a layer of oversight that international players typically require.

Expats living in Argentina should watch the shutdown mechanism closely. If passed, it could mean more austere public services when budgets run dry, but also a more predictable macroeconomic environment if the zero-deficit rule holds and inflation continues its downward trend.

Frequently Asked Questions

When will Argentina’s Central Bank reform be sent to Congress?

The government will announce the reform on 30 July 2026 and send it to Congress in early August 2026. The exact chamber of origin, whether the Senate or the Chamber of Deputies, has not yet been decided.

What are the main changes in the BCRA charter reform?

The reform establishes a single mandate of preserving the currency’s value, explicitly bans BCRA financing of the State at all levels, strengthens governance by requiring a two-thirds congressional majority to remove bank leadership, and eliminates non-transferable Treasury letters.

Which state-owned companies are being privatised in Argentina?

Under the Ley de Bases framework, eight companies are authorised for total or partial privatisation, including Aerolíneas Argentinas, Energía Argentina, Radio y Televisión Argentina, Intercargo, and water utility AySA. Four are already in the active pipeline, with five more under consideration.

World.title: Chile Private Mining to Pay Record US$8 Billion to State
World.content:
Chile Fiscal Windfall

Key Facts —Record payment. Private miners will pay US$8,039 million to the Chilean state in 2026, a 32% jump from 2025. —Budget share. The sum equals 9.1% of all projected central government revenues for the year. —Copper driver. High copper prices and strong export volumes are the main engine behind the record contribution. —Royalty effect. A new mining royalty law, fully active since 2024, adds roughly US$1.35 billion annually to state income. —Regional share. About US$450 million of the royalty revenue is legally earmarked for regional and municipal funds.

Chile private mining companies are projected to transfer a record US$8,039 million to government coffers in 2026, reshaping the fiscal landscape for Latin America’s richest mining economy.

Chile’s Private Mining to Deliver Record US$8 Billion to State Coffers (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

A Historic Payment Reshapes the Budget

Chile’s Budget Office (Dipres) has pencilled in US$8,039 million from large private mining operators for 2026. The figure marks the largest payment from the industry since records began.

The sum represents a 32% increase over 2025 private mining payments. It also shatters the previous record of US$6,207 million set during the commodity super-cycle of 2007.

Total central government revenues for 2026 are projected at US$88,842 million. Private mining alone will cover roughly 9.1% of that total, giving the sector outsized weight in national accounts.

Copper Remains the Undisputed Fiscal Engine

Copper is the dominant force behind the numbers. In the first half of 2026, copper exports reached US$30.236 billion, accounting for 50.1% of all Chilean exports.

The Ministry of Finance explicitly links the revenue jump to high copper prices and robust production volumes. Each US$0.01 per pound increase in the copper price adds an estimated US$27–35 million to fiscal revenues.

Copper provided 43% of all mining-related government revenue in 2024, a year when total mining income stood near US$5 billion. The 2026 projection shows that dependence intensifying rather than easing.

The New Royalty Law Delivers on Its Promise

A structural shift underpins the record. The Mining Royalty Law, fully in force from 2024, combines a 1% ad valorem tax on copper sales with a margin-based royalty of 8–26% on adjusted mining operating income.

The government estimates the law will generate about US$1.35 billion annually from 2025 onward, equivalent to 0.45% of GDP. The total tax burden for the largest producers is capped at 46.5% of operating profit.

Bank reports for 2025 already showed private mining revenues rising 47–50% year-on-year. Dipres projections simply extend that trend into 2026, confirming the royalty is working as designed.

Where the Money Goes: Regions Get a Guaranteed Slice

Not all the new revenue stays in Santiago. Roughly US$450 million of the annual royalty take is legally earmarked for regional and municipal funds.

The Regional Productivity and Development Fund receives about US$225 million. A Territorial Equity Fund for lower-income municipalities gets roughly US$170 million, while a Mining Municipalities Compensation Fund takes around US$55 million.

This distribution mechanism is designed to ease local opposition to mining projects. Communities that host operations now have a direct fiscal stake in the industry’s success.

Codelco and Lithium Add Further Fuel

The private sector is not the only contributor. State-owned Codelco is projected to transfer US$3,188 million to the state in 2026, its largest contribution in five years and a 58% real increase over 2025.

Lithium property rents administered via development agency Corfo are set to reach US$1,231 million, a 234% jump versus the prior year. Combined, total mining-related public revenue will comfortably exceed US$12 billion.

Mining accounts for 10–12% of Chile’s GDP and 50–60% of exports. The 2026 figures confirm the sector’s role as the irreplaceable backbone of public finance.

What Investors and Expats Should Watch Next

The record contribution signals a stable, rules-based fiscal framework for mining investors. The royalty law’s cap on total tax burden provides predictability that global boards value.

However, the heavy reliance on copper prices cuts both ways. Part of the windfall flows into the Economic and Social Stabilization Fund, a sovereign wealth vehicle designed to smooth budget swings when commodity cycles turn.

For expats and professionals in Santiago, the fiscal bounty could ease pressure on public services and infrastructure spending. The regional distribution of royalty funds may also unlock new opportunities in mining-adjacent communities across the north.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much will Chile private mining pay the state in 2026?

Chile’s Budget Office projects private mining companies will contribute US$8,039 million in 2026. This is a 32% increase over 2025 and the largest payment from the industry on record.

What is driving the record mining revenue in Chile?

High copper prices and strong export volumes are the main drivers. The new Mining Royalty Law, which combines an ad valorem tax and a margin-based royalty, is also contributing roughly US$1.35 billion annually from 2025 onward.

Where does the mining royalty money go in Chile?

About US$450 million of the annual royalty revenue is legally earmarked for regional and municipal funds. This includes money for a Regional Productivity and Development Fund, a Territorial Equity Fund for lower-income municipalities, and a compensation fund for mining communes.

World.title: OceanPact Buys Dock Brasil in a US$23 Million Ship-Repair Deal
World.content:
Brazilian Maritime Services

Key Facts —The price. OceanPact will pay a base price of R$119 million (US$23.1 million) for 100% of Dock Brasil. —The structure. The deal runs through OceanPact’s wholly owned subsidiary Estaleiro Farol de São Tomé, not the listed parent directly. —The conditions. Closing requires Dock Brasil to restructure and extinguish certain debts before the deal can complete. —The CBO merger. CADE approved the OceanPact-CBO combination without restrictions on 27 July, creating a 73-vessel offshore fleet. —The strategy. OceanPact aims to cut operating costs and strengthen vertical integration by internalising ship repair and maintenance.

OceanPact buys Dock Brasil for R$119 million, adding a dedicated ship repair yard just as regulators clear its blockbuster merger with CBO to create Brazil’s largest offshore support vessel operator.

OceanPact Buys Dock Brasil in R$119 Million Ship Repair Deal (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

What OceanPact buys Dock Brasil for and how the deal works

OceanPact Serviços Marítimos S.A. (OPCT3) disclosed on 28 July 2026 that its subsidiary Estaleiro Farol de São Tomé signed a binding contract to acquire 100% of Dock Brasil’s shares. The base price is approximately R$119 million, structured on a debt-free, cash-free basis.

The transaction remains subject to customary suspensive conditions, including the prior restructuring and extinguishment of certain Dock Brasil indebtedness. OceanPact has not yet disclosed a closing date or provided guidance on the timing for definitive completion.

The price includes standard update and adjustment mechanisms, along with price-retention arrangements to secure indemnification obligations agreed in the contract. Dock Brasil is described in coverage as an existing, operational naval repair infrastructure focused on ship repair, maintenance, and docking capacity.

Why OceanPact buys Dock Brasil now

OceanPact frames the acquisition as another step in its strategy to expand maritime infrastructure capabilities. The company expects to significantly increase its capacity to provide repair, maintenance, and docking services for both its own vessels and third-party client vessels.

The move aims to boost operational efficiency, reduce operating costs, and strengthen vertical integration by internalising repair and maintenance activities. OceanPact argues this will enhance its competitiveness in the Brazilian maritime services market through better control over support infrastructure.

The acquisition also positions the company to respond more quickly to growing demand for specialised services linked to offshore, port, and maritime support sectors. Incorporating an established, operational yard allows OceanPact to improve its service offering for an expanding fleet and client base.

The CBO merger clears, creating a 73-vessel offshore giant

Brazil’s antitrust authority CADE approved the OceanPact-CBO business combination without restrictions on 27 July 2026, one day before the Dock Brasil announcement. The combined company will operate 73 offshore support vessels with projected annual revenue above R$4 billion (US$778 million).

The all-stock deal will see OceanPact issue approximately 274 million to 275 million new shares to CBO’s shareholders. CBO shareholders will hold roughly 57.86% to 58% of the combined company, while existing OceanPact shareholders retain about 42% to 43%.

The combined backlog stands at about R$14 billion (US$2.7 billion), providing strong revenue visibility. OceanPact’s Investor Relations director indicated at the Brazil Investment Forum 2026 that roughly 95% of the company’s revenue comes from long-term contracts of three to four years, reducing exposure to oil price volatility.

OceanPact’s offshore services profile and what it means for investors

Founded in 2007 in Rio de Janeiro, OceanPact started as an environmental consulting and oil spill response firm before evolving into a broad maritime services group. It now serves oil and gas, ports, mining, energy, and telecom clients across three main business units: environmental protection, subsea services, and maritime logistics and engineering.

Chartering of maritime support vessels accounts for about 67% of total revenue, while services in marine environments contribute roughly 33%. The company maintains dedicated bases for environmental protection and offshore logistics, including one of the largest environmental protection bases in Latin America at Porto do Açu in Rio de Janeiro state.

Decommissioning has become a major growth avenue within OceanPact’s services segment, supported by a large Petrobras budget for decommissioning in the 2026-2030 period. The Dock Brasil acquisition adds in-house repair capacity that should improve margins on both its own fleet maintenance and third-party work.

What the Dock Brasil deal signals for Brazil’s maritime sector

The acquisition reflects a broader consolidation trend in Brazil’s offshore services industry, where scale and vertical integration increasingly determine competitiveness. OceanPact is building an integrated platform that spans vessel ownership, subsea operations, environmental response, and now dedicated repair infrastructure.

For international investors and expats watching Brazil’s maritime sector, the deal signals confidence in sustained offshore activity despite global energy transition pressures. The long-term contract profile and Petrobras’s decommissioning budgets provide a multi-year demand floor that makes infrastructure investments like Dock Brasil economically rational.

The timing is notable: securing repair capacity immediately after CADE cleared the CBO merger suggests OceanPact is moving quickly to capture synergies and prepare the combined fleet for efficient operations. Investors should watch for the debt restructuring milestone at Dock Brasil as the next concrete signal on deal completion.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is OceanPact paying for Dock Brasil?

OceanPact is paying a base price of approximately R$119 million (US$23.1 million) for 100% of Dock Brasil’s shares, on a debt-free, cash-free basis. The price is subject to customary adjustment mechanisms and price-retention arrangements to secure indemnification obligations.

What does Dock Brasil do and why does OceanPact want it?

Dock Brasil operates naval repair infrastructure focused on ship repair, maintenance, and docking services. OceanPact wants the yard to internalise these services, cutting operating costs and strengthening vertical integration across its growing fleet of 73 offshore support vessels following the CBO merger.

Has the OceanPact-CBO merger been approved?

Yes, Brazil’s antitrust authority CADE approved the OceanPact-CBO business combination without restrictions on 27 July 2026. The combined company will operate 73 offshore support vessels with projected annual revenue above R$4 billion and a backlog of approximately R$14 billion.

World.title: Liberia’s IMF Review Unlocks About US$50 Million for the Economy
World.content:
Africa · Western

Key Facts —IMF Board decision. On 27 April 2026, the IMF Executive Board approved a new Resilience and Sustainability Facility arrangement for Liberia. —Total package size. The RSF is worth SDR 193.8 million, approximately US$266 million, disbursed over 21 months. —Immediate cash unlocked. The third ECF review released an immediate disbursement of about US$26.5 million. —Short-term liquidity. Combined with parallel World Bank flows, roughly US$50 million in near-term cash becomes available. —Climate-macro link. The RSF explicitly ties long-term, low-interest financing to climate-resilience reforms.

Liberia’s latest IMF review has unlocked roughly US$50 million in short-term cash, anchoring the fragile West African economy to a Bretton Woods reform programme at a moment of intensifying global competition for influence.

Liberia: un accord avec le FMI ouvre la voie à un décaissement de 50 millions $ (Photo internet reproduction)
